**Checking the sign convention.** The Gaussian integration-by-parts step is the place where a sign error would matter. I tested it on a Brownian bridge on [0,1] tilted by e^{-λ∫ω ds}. There E_μ[ω(s)] = -λ s(1-s)/2, so g'' = λ = ∂U, which matches the proposed relation E[∫φ ∂U] = ∫φ g''. The top-layer case then gives A_1 = -g_1'' > 0, which is consistent. The general relation A_{n-1} - A_n = g_n'' is also consistent with this.

**Consistency of the recursion.** Summing the relations gives A_n = -∂²E[Σ_{k≤n} H_k] = -∂²E[log Z_n]. A stationary ensemble (g'' = 0) would force A_n = 0, which is impossible since the exponential is positive. So the ensemble must have a nonzero mean curvature, and the answer is determined by that curvature.

**Curvature.** The narrow-wedge Galilean shear Z(t,x)e^{vx+v²t/2} with Z(t,x+vt) preserves the initial data at t = 0, which gives E[H_1(x)] = c(t) - x²/(2t). Applying the same shear to the multilayer system shifts each layer by the same linear-plus-constant amount, so each layer has curvature -1/t. Summing n layers gives E[log Z_n] curvature -n/t, and therefore A_n = n/t. The result is also x-independent and decays as t → ∞, which is plausible.

**Remaining doubts.** The per-layer Galilean claim is the least rigorously justified step. I could not verify from memory that the Corwin–Hammond H-ensemble carries exactly this parabolic mean with the stated normalization. The internal consistency checks pass, so I accept the answer with moderate confidence.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
CONFIDENCE: 3
